title: Loop Mirror
experiment: Aharonov–Bohm effect in a Sagnac ring (loop mirror)
intro: This world is a ring: the left and right edges are portals, so whatever leaves on one side comes back on the other. A thin wall splits the packet in two. One half goes round the ring to the right, the other to the left, and both come back to the wall from opposite sides at the same moment. With nothing else in the world the wall then sends everything back where it came from, onto the mine: the ring is a mirror. A magnetic flux runs through the hole of the ring, where the particle never goes. Dial it so the ring lets the particle through instead.
goal: Set the flux Φ through the ring (in flux quanta Φ₀ = h/e) so that, when the world looks at t = 22, the particle is past the wall (green) rather than back where it started (red).

physics.point: A flux the particle never touches still shifts the phase of every trip round the ring by 2πΦ/Φ₀. The two halves go round in opposite senses, so their phases differ by twice that: a quarter flux quantum turns the mirror into a window.

idea: In 1959 Aharonov and Bohm pointed out that an electron going round a solenoid feels the magnetic flux inside it, although the field outside is zero: the vector potential shifts the phase of every path that winds round the flux. Tonomura's electron holography confirmed it in 1986 with a superconducting ring that shut the field in completely.

A ring with a beam splitter in it is a Sagnac interferometer. The two halves travel the same loop in opposite directions, so any ordinary change to the loop (its length, a slab of potential) affects both equally and cancels. With nothing to tell them apart they recombine into the port they came from: a loop mirror, used in fibre optics.

The flux does tell them apart. Going round with the vector potential adds +2πΦ/Φ₀ to one half and −2πΦ/Φ₀ to the other. At Φ = Φ₀/4 their phase difference is π and the wall sends them on, through the ring. Rotating the ring does the same thing to light (the Sagnac effect in a fibre gyroscope).
maths: With the portals the box is a ring of length L = 40. A flux Φ is a twist: ψ(x + L) = e^{iθ}ψ(x) with θ = 2πΦ/Φ₀, equivalently a kinetic momentum p = k + θ/L, which the solver uses exactly. The packet is launched with the same physical speed for every Φ, so only the phase per lap changes.

The wall (height 5) transmits about half at this speed. Each half makes one full lap, in opposite senses, and their relative phase is 2θ. At the second pass through the wall the output towards the target is ∝ sin²θ and back towards the mine ∝ cos²θ, so the response repeats every half flux quantum:
The rest of the probability is still on its way or spread in y. The wall's transmission depends on speed, so the halves are not exactly equal and the mirror is not perfect.
try: Flux 0: watch the two halves leave in opposite directions, pass through the portals, and meet at the wall; nearly all of it comes back to the left.
Flux 0.25: the same two halves, the same paths, but the meeting sends them right.
Flux 0.5: back to a mirror, a full period of the Sagnac response.
